doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Black musicians at Curtis and in the Philadelphia Orchestra
summary: Gold recalls Wilmer Wise, Weldon Berry and Renard Edwards, who joined the Philadelphia Orchestra at 18.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Were there any black students when you were there? Because I know Joe Wilder and some other black musicians went there. This would have been years before you.
Well Joe Wilder has passed now, but this would have been in the mid—'40s.
I don't even know Joe Wilder. Who is Joe Wilder?
Joe Wilder is a wonderful trumpet player. And he aspired to a classical career but there was no such thing for him.
Yeah. I know. I knew a Wilmer Wise. You know the name Wilmer Wise?

Look him up. He was Leonard Bernstein's first call for like when he did his Broadway shows, you know, in that pit band he was Leonard Bernstein's first call. Brilliant violin — he was also Pablo Casals' first call in the Bach orchestra suites at Marlboro. He was a brilliant musician. I don't think he went to Curtis. When I was there there was a young man who played the clarinet named Weldon Berry who was from Philadelphia, who was a black clarinet player. And my best friend growing up was Renard Edwards who is a little older than me and still a member of the Philadelphia Orchestra. He got in the Philadelphia Orchestra at age 18, left I don't know whether he was at Curtis or he was before Curtis, but Philly Orchestra had to add a few black players and some women because they were going to lose some grants and so all of a sudden Renard came home and said, "I'm a member of the Philadelphia Orchestra." I just saw him recently and I
have to say for someone who is 80 years old he still looked brilliant and still plays and that viola is so heavy and I don't understand how he can still do it.
